name: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation)
description: POPE is a polling-based object probing evaluation benchmark for assessing object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about objects in images (e.g., 'Is there a car in the image?'). The dataset is built on MSCOCO validation images and supports three sampling strategies: Random, Popular, and Adversarial. It also supports extension to unannotated datasets via automatic segmentation tools like SEEM.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
publisher: Renmin University of China, Meituan Group
citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3 [cs.CV], 26 Oct 2023.
rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset is constructed from the MSCOCO validation set. 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects in annotations are randomly selected for POPE evaluation. For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions are randomly sampled from the MSCOCO validation set. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or via automatic segmentation using SEEM. The dataset is also extended to A-OKVQA and GQA using SEEM-based automatic annotation.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: MSCOCO (Microsoft Common Objects in Context) validation set, including images with ground-truth object annotations and human-labeled captions. Additional datasets used include A-OKVQA and GQA, annotated using the SEEM automatic segmentation tool.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative object sampling strategies are applied to construct polling questions: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects not present in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones not present in the image. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance. Six questions are constructed per image (l=6).
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR evaluation, only the 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge are considered, following Rohrbach et al. (2018). For POPE, images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are selected. For SEEM-based POPE, automatic segmentation results are used to identify objects in unannotated datasets. ChatGPT is used to parse open-ended LVLM responses for VQA evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object annotations are taken from existing MSCOCO human annotations. For unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA, GQA), automatic segmentation using SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) is used to generate object labels. Polling questions are formulated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?' with binary Yes/No answers.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic segmentation-based annotation; MSCOCO human annotation for ground-truth labels.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and model-generated captions was validated. Out of 1303 and 1445 objects given 'No' responses by InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4 respectively, merely 0 and 5 were referenced in captions. Out of 664 and 1034 objects mentioned in captions, 664 and 961 received 'Yes' verdicts, confirming strong correlation between caption content and POPE responses.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 polling questions per image (3 ground-truth objects, 3 nonexistent objects)
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic object segmentation and annotation; ChatGPT for parsing open-ended LVLM responses in VQA evaluation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications. For example, an autonomous driving system with incorrect understanding of the external environment could make wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The work also highlights risks for blind users relying on computer-generated image captions.
rai:dataBiases: The visual instruction datasets of LVLMs are mostly constructed based on MSCOCO, which has an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. LVLMs fine-tuned on such data are prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects. Additionally, frequently co-occurring object groups contribute to hallucination bias. The CHAIR metric is sensitive to instruction design and caption length, which can bias evaluation results.
rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on coarse-grained object hallucination and does not consider fine-grained aspects such as object number, attributes, and positions. Evaluation is conducted on a subset of the validation set due to computational resource limitations, which may be affected by data distribution. The matching-based method for determining Yes/No answers may fail when LVLMs do not explicitly use these words. When using automatic segmentation tools, object labels may be inconsistent with human annotations. Only a small number of LVLMs are evaluated, excluding some recently released or closed-source models. POPE cannot measure overall LVLM performance.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in large vision-language models. The dataset supports benchmarking of LVLMs on hallucination under three difficulty settings (Random, Popular, Adversarial). It can also be extended to unannotated datasets for scalable evaluation. Not recommended as a sole measure of overall LVLM capability.
